title: I wanted a Gauntlet style game with modern ARPG loot systems. From there Hordebreaker was born.
author: whatisinaname513
selftext:
https://eviepuffroo.itch.io/hordebreaker

DEVLOG #1 · In development DEMO Release

Welcome to the Starlite Arcade

Hi, and thank you for dropping a coin in. Hordebreaker is open for early access testing, and whether you played one floor or forty, I'm glad you're here.

The setup: the Starlite Arcade closes tonight. The auction truck comes at 6:00 AM, and one cabinet isn't on the auction list. It's on the scrap list, and it knows. While someone is playing it, it's sure it exists, so it would really like you to keep playing.

That cabinet is the game. This first post covers what Hordebreaker is, where it comes from, and then goes deep on a few systems I'm proud of. If you only read one part, read the last section: I want to hear from you.

What you're playing

Hordebreaker is a top-down horde crawler. It has classic arcade bones and a modern looter's appetite. A run looks like this:

Floors full of monsters. Generators keep pumping enemies out until you break them, so you learn to kill the spawners first and kite the rest through loops and choke points.

Food, keys and vaults. Your health drains slowly, so food matters. Keys open gold-doored vaults full of chests.

A boss every third floor, twelve in all, each with a named signature attack.

Level-ups draft boons (pick one of three), and gear drops with affixes, sets, sockets and runes.

The Coin-Op sits between floors: spend your gold on gear, a meal, a key or a continue.

Credits. Dying offers a continue, so a great build doesn't end on one mistake.

There are 14 heroes. Five play the way you'd hope (Warrior, Ranger, Wizard, Valkyrie, Rogue). 

The other nine each bend the game into a different genre: a level editor, a time puzzle, a physics sandbox, a deckbuilder, a rhythm game, a tower defense, a possession game, a reverse horde, and a speedrunner's bug. After a boss you can find a Cartridge Slot and fuse a second class into yours.

Past the main run there's an endless endgame from floor 17, bonus stages, DIP switches for harder runs and better tickets, a Prize Counter, and three neighbouring cabinets you can stumble into: a synthwave racer with three tracks, a street fighter and a lunar platformer.

Where it comes from

Hordebreaker started from one question: what if the arcade dungeon crawlers I grew up with had a modern loot game's depth, and the dungeon itself was something you could break?

Gauntlet is the spine: generators, food, keys, potions that clear the screen, credits, and an announcer who will absolutely tell you when you need food.

Action RPG loot is the gear game: affixes, rarities, item sets, socketed runes and signature legendaries that change how a class plays.

Modern roguelites gave me the level-up boon draft, and boons that evolve when you find the right pair.

The 1980s arcade is the whole presentation: CRT fonts, a cabinet frame with a marquee and a coin door, a synthwave soundtrack, and the machines next door.

Games that know they're games. The cabinet is a character. It has a night clock, DIP switches, a logbook left by the staff, and opinions about being unplugged.

Four rules sit under every feature. If a feature serves none of them, it gets cut:

Hordes, not encounters. The screen should fill up. You thin a crowd rather than clearing one room at a time.

Earned overpowerment. Early floors are a real fight. Monster health grows linearly while a good build grows multiplicatively, and that gap is the power trip.

The level is a toy. Walls can be raised, bored, collapsed and thrown.

Arcade clarity, modern depth. You should understand it in ten seconds and still be finding builds after a hundred hours.

Under the hood

This is the nerdy part. If you just want to play, skip to the end. Otherwise, here's how some of the stranger systems work.

One grid, many classes

Several classes rewrite the dungeon mid-fight. The Architect raises walls on top of monsters, the Glitch noclips through them, the Gravity Knight throws the horde into them. That only works because there is exactly one source of truth: the floor is a single tile grid, and every change goes through one function. Change a tile and pathfinding, collision, rendering, the wall cutaway and the minimap all update from it. No class owns private geometry.

Monsters navigate with a flow field rather than per-monster pathfinding: one pass from the player outward gives every tile a direction toward you. Two hundred monsters cost the pathfinder about the same as two, and when a wall falls, the field is rebuilt and the whole horde pours through the new gap.

The classes that bend the level follow a hard rule: no softlocks. The map border can't be touched, the exit always stays reachable, and Noclip always picks a legal landing tile. Every floor is checked as it's built, too. The generator walks the map from the start, refills any pocket it can't reach and remembers the walkable tiles, and everything that spawns (generators, keys, pickups, objectives) picks from that list. Before shipping that change I ran 1,800 generated maps and 180 full floor builds without a single unreachable spawn.

Walls have hit points

Every wall that faces open floor has health, set by the biome's material and rising 12% per floor.

Shots that die on a wall deal half their damage to it, explosions fall off toward their edge, and dashing into a wall counts. A wall cracks below 66%, crumbles below 33% and falls at zero, throwing rubble in the direction of the hit. Two guard rails keep it fair: no single hit takes more than 60% of a fresh wall, and a wall hit again within 0.09 seconds takes only a quarter, so a hose of tiny hits can't melt the level.

Behind every breakable wall is bedrock, tinted cold blue-grey. Destruction opens a wall between two spaces, never a tunnel through the mountain. That keeps vaults sealed, boss arenas closed and the map border intact.

Physics plugs into this. Monsters knocked into a wall hard enough damage it and take an impact hit themselves, scaled by their speed. The Gravity Knight's Tilt the World points gravity wherever you aim for five seconds (after a half-second warning arrow on the floor), and the horde slides, slams into walls, and gets stunned. Enemy bullets curve with it, and loot slides toward you.

A soundtrack you can fight to

There are no audio files in Hordebreaker. Every song is synthesized live by a small sequencer in the browser: drums, bass, chords and lead, with layers that build as a fight heats up and a theme for every biome and boss.

Because the game writes its own music, it knows exactly where the beat is. The Conductor reads a beat clock from the soundtrack itself, with audio latency compensated, so the rhythm game is real:

Baton Bolts fire on the music's eighth notes, and each one plays a note of the chord that's playing.

Downbeat is a shockwave you tap on the beat. A PERFECT (within ±75 ms) hits three times as hard as an off-beat tap; a GOOD (±150 ms) hits twice as hard.

On-beat play builds Groove, +15% damage a level up to four. Off-beat play breaks it.

Crescendo throws a shockwave on every beat for two bars, ends on a fortissimo blast, and pushes the music to full intensity.

The Glitch is a bug in the cabinet

The Glitch is my favourite class to explain. In the fiction, the dungeon runs on an arcade board and the Glitch is a fault in it. Its tools are bugs:

Lag Spike freeze-frames an area for 2.5 seconds. Damage dealt to anything lagged isn't applied. It's buffered at 1.5× and lands all at once as a DESYNC hit when the lag ends.

Noclip dashes straight through walls and lags whatever it phases through.

Kill Screen corrupts a field for six seconds, then releases everything it stored in one burst.

Corrupted loot. 30% of the Glitch's drops roll with every affix doubled plus one bug, a real drawback like slower movement. You decide whether it's worth wearing.

Making skills matter: Focus, Surge and Overdrive

In a horde game it's tempting to hold the attack button forever. A few systems push back on that.

Focus charges from basic attacks, shown as three pips on your skill. Each hit adds up to 0.1 of a pip, but from a budget that refills at only 0.45 a second. Steady fire fills all three pips in about five seconds, and one giant area attack can't fill them in a single frame. Casting your skill spends every full pip: +30% skill damage per pip for four seconds (+90% at three, which the game calls EMPOWERED). The cast also Surges your basic attack, which fires faster and harder for a couple of seconds. So the rhythm is attack, cast, attack.

Overdrive, your ultimate, charges from the share of each enemy's health you remove. Overkill doesn't count and tougher enemies are worth more. The fill rate is capped (never faster than 25 seconds from empty), so even a maxed-out build can't chain ultimates back to back.

Late game adds pressure. From floor 7 basic attacks taper a little each floor while skills keep their full weight, and from floor 10 champions and bosses are warded against basic attacks until a skill or Overdrive cracks them open.

Everything is made in code

Hordebreaker is three.js in a browser tab, and nearly all of it is generated: the heroes and monsters are sculpted from primitives with crease shading baked in, the textures are procedural, the soundtrack is the live synth above, and every floor is generated fresh. The whole game zips to under a megabyte.

Early access: help me make it better

This is a work in progress, and I mean that literally. Balance moves every week, some systems are first drafts, and you will find bugs. I'm sharing it now because it's fun, and because the best improvements so far have come straight from playtest notes. The portal that used to swallow you before you could grab the boss loot, the forest of loot beams, and the skeleton army that tanked the frame rate were all reported by playtesters and fixed.

Please leave a comment. Short notes are just as welcome as essays. These are the things I most want to know:

Difficulty. Where did a run get too easy, too hard, or too long? Which floor were you on?

Classes. Which hero felt strongest, which felt weak, and which one confused you?

Readability. Did you ever lose track of your hero, an enemy shot or a pickup in a big fight?

Performance. Your frame rate, browser and graphics card help a lot. Options has HD graphics, Model detail and Auto quality if it's struggling.

Bugs. What happened, what you expected, and the class and floor, if you remember.

The best moment. I'd love to know what made you grin.

A few things to know going in:

It plays best in a desktop browser (Chrome, Edge or Firefox) with a keyboard and mouse or a gamepad.

Your progress saves in your browser, and a run can be continued after you close the tab.

The first runs teach one system at a time. If something isn't explained when you need it, that's feedback too.

Thank you for playing, for breaking things, and for telling me about it. The truck is coming at six, so keep the lights on as long as you can.

See you on the high score table.

replies.body:
That's been one of the consistent things I've been tinkering with. This video is not the best, I'll admit. I need to record gameplay locally and edit, rather than have Claude Code render the whole thing. Loot filters help a lot to declutter the visual field and in full screen the effect isn't as pronounced. Still, I've played around with amount of loot that drops, the amount of monsters that spawn, etc. The quick cuts do make it look worse in the video, too.

It's helpful to get the feedback, even if (I'm assuming) from only watching a video of gameplay.

It's a fine line I'm not always sure I'm on the correct side of...

replies.author: whatisinaname513
replies.body:
Yes, for sure. Or something similar. I only had the youtube clip handy since itch.io requires one for the trailer. 

I need to make some good marketing videos of all the different systems and features. I'm bad at marketing...but hey it's free to try out!
